questions.q: In the regex `r"<(?P<pri>\d+)>..."` used to parse a syslog line, what does the `(?P<pri>...)` syntax provide?
options: A named capture group, letting you access the matched value by name (e.g. match.groupdict()["pri"]) instead of a numeric index
A way to tell Python to ignore that part of the string entirely
A built-in syslog parser bundled with Python's standard library
A case-insensitive match flag for that portion of the pattern
questions.explain: Named groups let you pull matched substrings out of a regex by name via groupdict(), which is far more readable than numbered groups for downstream processing.

questions.q: What is the most common practical trap when working with JSON security logs from multiple vendors, according to the lesson?
options: JSON Lines files cannot be read line by line in Python
JSON logs cannot contain numeric severity values
The json module cannot parse nested objects
Inconsistent field names and value shapes across vendors (e.g. severity vs Severity vs properties.level)
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes that the real JSON parsing trap isn't syntax -- it's that different vendors use different field names and value encodings for the same concept, requiring normalization before correlation.

questions.q: When opening a CSV security export in Python with csv.DictReader, why does the lesson recommend passing newline="" to open()?
options: It automatically converts the file to UTF-8 encoding
It prevents Windows-style line endings from producing blank or malformed rows on some platforms
It is required for csv.DictReader to exist at all
It forces all values to be read as integers
questions.explain: The lesson notes that omitting newline="" can cause blank rows or line-ending issues depending on platform; it does not affect encoding or data types.

questions.q: A CSV row read with csv.DictReader has a column "confidence" containing the text "85". What type is that value in Python before you do anything else to it?
options: A boolean, True
An integer, 85
A string, "85"
A float, 85.0
questions.explain: csv.DictReader reads every field as a string regardless of what it looks like; you must explicitly convert it (e.g. int(row["confidence"])) to use it numerically.

questions.q: Why does the lesson stress converting all timestamps to a single timezone-aware UTC standard before correlating events from different sources?
options: Because CSV files cannot contain timestamp data at all
Because Python's datetime module cannot store any timezone other than UTC
Because UTC is required by the json module to parse timestamp fields
Because syslog, JSON, and CSV formats represent time differently, and comparing unnormalized timestamps can make events that happened hours apart look simultaneous, or vice versa
questions.explain: The lesson explains that skipping timestamp normalization is a common cause of silently wrong correlation results, since different formats represent time differently (local time, ISO 8601 with offset, MM/DD/YYYY, etc.).
